chapters.n: Habakkuk is unique: instead of speaking for God to the people, he questions God on behalf of the people. He lived in Judah shortly before Babylon’s invasion, around 605 BC — in the same era as Lehi and Jeremiah.

f.g: A weighty prophetic message.
The name may mean “embrace” or come from a word for a garden plant.

chapters.n: Habakkuk’s honest complaint: “Lord, how long must I cry for help before You listen? I cry ‘Violence!’ and You don’t save.” Scripture shows it is okay to bring our hard questions to God.
Why does God make him watch injustice? Everywhere he looks there is destruction, violence, and conflict in Judah.

f.g: Trouble, misery.
Plundering, destruction.

chapters.n: Because of this, the law is paralyzed and justice never wins. The wicked surround the righteous, so justice comes out twisted.

f.g: The law is numb, ineffective.
Perverted, crooked justice.

chapters.n: God answers: Look among the nations and be amazed! I am doing something in your lifetime you wouldn’t believe even if told. Paul quoted this as a warning against rejecting the gospel.

f.w: I will work a work in your days

chapters.n: The surprise: God is raising up the Chaldeans (Babylonians) — a fierce, swift nation that will sweep through the land seizing homes that aren’t theirs. God uses even pagan powers to discipline His people.

f.g: The ruling people of the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar.

chapters.n: They are terrifying and answer to no one; they make their own rules and honor only themselves.

f.w: their judgment and their dignity shall proceed of themselves
f.g: They are a law unto themselves.

chapters.n: Their horses are faster than leopards and fiercer than wolves hunting at dusk. Their cavalry swoops in from far away like eagles diving on prey.

f.g: Wolves hungry after a day without food, hunting at dusk.

f.w: they shall fly as the eagle

chapters.n: They come intent on violence, sweeping forward like the desert wind, gathering captives as countless as sand.

f.w: their faces shall sup up as the east wind
f.g: Their faces press forward like a scorching desert wind.

chapters.n: They laugh at kings and scoff at fortresses, simply piling up earth ramps to capture them.

f.g: Build siege ramps of earth against city walls.

chapters.n: They sweep on like the wind, but they are guilty — they make their own strength their god.

f.w: imputing this his power unto his god
f.g: Treating their own might as divine.

chapters.n: Habakkuk responds: Lord, You are eternal and holy. We will not die. You have appointed Babylon to correct us, our Rock.

f.g: Ancient scribes say the original read “You do not die”; either way it affirms God’s eternal nature.
Literally “O Rock” — a title of steadfast strength.

chapters.n: His deeper question: You are too pure to look on evil, so how can You stay silent while the wicked swallow up people more righteous than they?

f.w: Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil

chapters.n: God seems to treat people like fish or bugs with no leader to protect them.

f.g: Small crawling creatures.

chapters.n: The Babylonians haul in nations like a fisherman with hooks and nets — and they rejoice over their catch.

f.g: Fishhook.
Dragnet.

chapters.n: They worship their nets — their military power — because it makes them rich and well-fed.

f.g: Idolizing their tools of conquest.

chapters.n: Will they keep emptying their nets and killing nations forever? Habakkuk’s question hangs, awaiting God’s answer in chapter 2.

f.g: Keep on slaughtering without mercy.

chapters.n: Habakkuk takes his post like a watchman on a tower, waiting for God’s reply. After asking hard questions, he waits patiently for revelation.

f.w: I will stand upon my watch

f.g: Corrected — or answered regarding his complaint.

chapters.n: The Lord answers: write the vision clearly on tablets so a messenger can read it easily as he runs to spread it.

f.g: Tablets — clay, stone, or wood writing surfaces.

f.w: that he may run that readeth it
f.g: So that a herald can read it quickly and carry it.

chapters.n: The vision is for an appointed time. It may seem slow, but wait — it will surely come. God’s timing is certain even when it isn’t ours.

f.w: though it tarry, wait for it

chapters.n: The heart of the book: the proud are not upright, but the righteous will live by faith — or faithfulness. Paul built his teaching on this verse.

f.w: the just shall live by his faith

f.g: Hebrew emunah — steady faithfulness, trust that holds firm.

chapters.n: The arrogant conqueror, like a drunk who never stays home, is as greedy as the grave — never satisfied, gathering all nations to himself.

f.g: Sheol, the grave, which always swallows more.

chapters.n: The first of five “woes”: the conquered nations will taunt Babylon. Woe to the one who piles up stolen goods and loads himself with debts. How long can that last?

f.g: A mocking song.
Heavy pledges or debts — piles of goods taken as collateral.

chapters.n: Suddenly the victims will rise up like creditors; they will plunder the plunderer.

f.g: There’s a pun: “biters” also means “creditors” (those who charge interest).
Plunder, spoils.

chapters.n: Because Babylon looted many nations, the survivors will loot it, for all its bloodshed and violence.

f.w: all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee

chapters.n: Second woe: to those who build their homes with dishonest gain, trying to set their nest high out of reach of disaster.
By destroying many peoples, they have brought shame on their own house and forfeited their own life.

f.g: Endangered or forfeited your own life.

chapters.n: The very stones and beams of their mansions will cry out as witnesses against them, since they were built with stolen wealth.

f.w: the stone shall cry out of the wall

chapters.n: Third woe: to those who build a city with blood and injustice.
The Lord has decreed that empires built this way labor only to fuel the fire, wearing themselves out for nothing.
A glorious contrast: someday the whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord’s glory, as water fills the sea. Human empires pass; God’s glory endures.

f.w: the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD

chapters.n: Fourth woe: to one who gets a neighbor drunk to shame and exploit him. Babylon intoxicated and humiliated nations.
Babylon will be filled with shame instead of glory. It must drink the cup of the Lord’s judgment and be exposed in disgrace.

f.w: the cup of the LORD's right hand

f.g: Be exposed as uncircumcised — outside God’s covenant.

chapters.n: The violence Babylon did to Lebanon’s forests and wildlife will come back on it, along with the bloodshed against people and cities.

f.g: Babylon cut Lebanon’s cedars for its buildings and hunted its wildlife.

chapters.n: What good is an idol made by human hands? It teaches only lies. The maker trusts in a speechless object he made himself.

f.g: Mute, unable to speak.

chapters.n: Fifth woe: to those who tell wood, “Wake up!” and stone, “Teach us!” It may be covered in gold, but it has no breath of life.

f.w: there is no breath at all in the midst of it

chapters.n: In contrast to silent idols, the living Lord is in His holy temple. Let the whole earth be silent before Him in reverence.

f.w: the LORD is in his holy temple
let all the earth keep silence before him

chapters.n: Habakkuk ends with a prayer set to music, like a psalm. His questions have turned into worship.

f.g: A musical term of uncertain meaning, perhaps an emotional, wandering style of song (see Psalm 7 heading).

chapters.n: Habakkuk is awed by what God has revealed. He asks the Lord to renew His mighty works in their own day — and, in wrath, to remember mercy.

f.g: Renew Your saving deeds, as in the past.

chapters.n: Habakkuk recalls God marching from the south, from Teman and Mount Paran, as when He came to Israel at Sinai. His glory fills the heavens.

f.g: A region in Edom, south of Judah.
A musical or liturgical marker, perhaps meaning a pause.

chapters.n: His brightness is like sunlight, with rays flashing from His hand — and still that is only the hiding place of His full power.

f.g: Rays of light (the same Hebrew word as for horns).
Even this blinding light veils His full power.

chapters.n: Plague and fiery bolts go before and after Him, as in the plagues of Egypt.

f.g: Or “pestilence/fever” — a second plague image.

chapters.n: He stands and the earth shakes; nations scatter and ancient mountains crumble. His ways are eternal.

f.g: Or “shook the earth.”

chapters.n: Desert peoples — Cushan and Midian — trembled in their tents when God came.

f.g: Probably a tribe related to Midian, in the southern wilderness.

chapters.n: Was God angry with the rivers and sea when He rode out in His chariots of salvation? Habakkuk recalls the parting of the Red Sea and the Jordan.
God uncovered His bow, fulfilling His sworn promises, and split the earth with rivers.

f.w: according to the oaths of the tribes, even thy word
f.g: One of the hardest lines in the Old Testament to translate; perhaps “arrows sworn by Your word.”

chapters.n: The mountains writhed, torrents swept by, and the deep roared and lifted its waves like hands.

f.w: The mountains saw thee, and they trembled

chapters.n: Sun and moon stood still at the flash of His arrows and spear — recalling Joshua’s long day.

f.w: The sun and moon stood still

chapters.n: In anger God marched through the earth and trampled the nations like grain on a threshing floor.

f.g: Trample, as oxen trample grain.

chapters.n: God went out to save His people and His anointed, crushing the leader of the wicked and laying him bare from head to foot.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ — the anointed king, or Israel itself; Christians see a hint of the Messiah.

f.w: discovering the foundation unto the neck
f.g: Stripping him bare from foundation to neck.

chapters.n: God turned the enemy’s own weapons against them. They had rushed in like a storm to scatter God’s people, gloating like those who devour the helpless in secret.

f.g: Spears or clubs.

chapters.n: God trampled the sea with His horses, churning the great waters, as at the Exodus.

f.w: Thou didst walk through the sea

chapters.n: Hearing all this, Habakkuk trembles to his bones. Yet he will wait quietly for the day of trouble to come on the invaders.

f.g: His strength drained away from fear.
Or “I will wait quietly.”

chapters.n: One of scripture’s great expressions of faith: even if the fig tree, vines, olives, fields, flocks, and herds all fail — every source of livelihood gone —

f.g: Food.

f.w: the fig tree shall not blossom

chapters.n: — yet I will rejoice in the Lord and find joy in the God who saves me. Faith does not depend on circumstances. Habakkuk moves from “How long?” to “Yet I will rejoice.”

f.w: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD

chapters.n: The Lord gives strength and makes Habakkuk sure-footed as a deer on mountain heights — able to stand firm in hard places. The note at the end directs the song to the choir leader.

f.w: he will make my feet like hinds' feet

f.g: Female deer, famously sure-footed on steep cliffs.
The music director, as in many psalm headings.
